claims.text: Q235 is a mild, low-carbon steel.
The pre-exposure Q235 reference has no pre-existing passivating film.
A dense, adherent Fe3O4 film governs the suppression or onset of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel.
Controlled low-temperature oxidation in an oxygen-rich atmosphere can form a uniform, dense magnetite film on Q235 steel.
The proposed controlled study compares magnetite-pretreated Q235 samples with untreated Q235 references.
Moisture and temperature can affect corrosion behavior.
Magnetite-film density, uniformity, porosity, and adhesion are the structural properties mediating corrosion protection.
A well-formed magnetite layer limits oxygen and moisture ingress into Q235 steel.
Limiting oxygen and moisture ingress reduces the electrochemical reactions driving corrosion.
The engineered magnetite film remains stable and protective at approximately 25°C.
At elevated temperature, the magnetite film develops greater porosity or spalls.
Elevated-temperature porosity or spallation permits accelerated corrosive attack.
At approximately 25°C, magnetite-pretreated Q235 will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated Q235.
At approximately 25°C, magnetite-pretreated Q235 will exhibit less surface degradation than untreated Q235.
At approximately 80°C, the pretreated film will become less adherent and the corrosion rates of treated and untreated samples will converge.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to oxygen- and moisture-driven corrosion when aggressive ions such as chloride are absent or minimized.
The proposed mechanism is applicable over moderate temperatures up to approximately 100°C.
Weight loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarization, SEM, and XPS can be used to compare corrosion kinetics and film quality in the controlled study.
Failure of the pretreatment to reduce room-temperature corrosion relative to the untreated control would falsify the proposed protective-film mechanism.
Retention of comparable protection at elevated temperature would falsify the predicted elevated-temperature loss of protective capacity.
